text.en:
Every year Raju's father sowed rice when the monsoon rains came and wheat when the winter began.
"Different crops like different seasons," he said, "and our fields give two harvests."

Farming in India depends on the seasons. Kharif crops such as rice, maize and cotton are sown with the monsoon in June-July and harvested in autumn. Rabi crops such as wheat, gram and mustard are sown in winter and harvested in spring.
Plants need water. Where rain is not enough, farmers irrigate the fields using wells, tube wells, tanks and canals. Modern methods such as drip irrigation save water.
In the 1960s the Green Revolution brought high-yielding seeds, fertilisers and irrigation, and food grain production rose. Today farmers also care about soil health, so some practise organic farming.
Kharif crops are sown with the monsoon. Rice and cotton are kharif crops.
Rabi crops are sown in winter. Wheat and mustard are rabi crops.
Farmers irrigate fields with wells, tanks and canals.
The Green Revolution raised food grain production in the 1960s.

problem.en: A farmer wants to grow wheat. When should he sow it and why?

text.en: So he sows it in winter, around October-November.

why.en: Rabi crops are harvested in spring.

prompt.en: A friend says all crops are grown at the same time of year. How will you reply?

requiredIdeas.en: Kharif crops are sown with the monsoon.
Rabi crops are sown in winter.

points.en: Kharif crops are sown in the monsoon and rabi crops in winter.
